title: Association of the hsCRP–Glycemia Index with Coronary Artery Occlusion in Diabetic Patients with STEMI
content: Background: The coexistence of elevated hs-CRP levels and diabetes mellitus may play a significant role in plaque destabilization, favoring plaque rupture and thrombosis, and consequently increasing the risk of coronary artery occlusion and acute coronary syndrome. Purpose: This study aimed to assess the CRP-glycemia index as potential predictors of of coronary artery occlusion in diabetic patients with acute coronary syndrome. Methods: The study included 131 consecutive patients presenting with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) within 12 hours of symptom onset who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). At admission, laboratory assessments were performed, including creatine kinase (CK), CK-MB, troponin I, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), glucose, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, cholesterol, and standard biochemical parameters. The CRP–glycemia index (CRPGI) was calculated using the formula: CRPGI = CRP (mg/L) × glucose (mmol/L). Based on the presence of coronary artery occlusion, patients were stratified into two groups: those with acute coronary syndrome and total coronary artery occlusion (ACS/CA-total occlusion (TO), Group 1) and those with ACS and non-total coronary artery occlusion (ACS/CA-non-total occlusion (nTO), Group 2). Results: Of the 131 diabetic patients with STEMI treated with PCI, 77 (58.77) had ACS/CA-TO (Group 1), while 54 (41.22%) had ACS/CA-nTO (Group 2) (Table 1). CRPGI differed significantly between the groups, p<0.0001. Significant differences were also observed in glucose, hs-CRP levels, CK, CK-MB, troponin I, and ejection fraction (EF) (p=0.011, p<0.0001, p<0.0001, p<0.000, p=0.004 and p<0.0001, respectively). Based on binary logistic regression, we analyzed the relationship between one dichotomous dependent variable (ACS/CA-TO or ACS/CA-nTO) and other variables (age hypertension, BMI, diabetes mellitus, smoking, glucose, hs-CRP, and CRP–glycemia index (CRPGI). Glucose, hs-CRP, and CRPGI are significant predictors at the 5% level, with p-values of 0.007, <0.0001 and <0.0001 respectively (Table 2). The ROC analysis of the CRPGI demonstrates an AUC of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.80–0.93), with an optimal threshold of 201.49 (p < 0.0001) (Table 3). Table 3 further summarizes the AUCs for the other biomarkers included in the study. Figure 1 presents the ROC curve analyses for the studied biomarkers, showing a progressive increase in predictive significance from glucose to CRP and finally to the CRP–glycemia index (CRPGI). Conclusions: The CRP–glycemia index (CRPGI) appears to be a valuable predictor of coronary artery occlusion in diabetic patients with STEMI, highlighting its potential utility for risk stratification and early clinical assessment.
